# Stack 03b — the canvas

**Waiting on Kent — nothing.** Every open item on this plan was answered on 2026-09-17. Three answers changed the design and are written into the body below: **provenance leaves the wire's stroke and becomes a three-step origin mark at the wire's tail**; **the diff view shows structure only until the engine's world route exists**, so there is no committed illustrative world and no "illustrative numbers" chip; and **the range under a number now means something specific** — how sure we are of the number, not how much the world can move — which the chip label, its hover sentence and the delta rail's new `agreement` column all have to say out loud (decision record 0014). The rest were accepted as written. Everything is marked **Kent, 2026-09-17** in the pre-decisions table.

---

**Goal:** the Hormuz map drawn so well that Kent wants to look at it. Tiles you can read, wires that show what kind of push they carry, a layout that never becomes a hairball, a panel that answers "why is this number what it is", and two worlds laid over each other so the change is obvious. Driven entirely by `GET /api/fixtures/hormuz`, which already works.

**What this stack must not do.** No model. No engine arithmetic — not one line that adds a strength, evaluates a shape or multiplies a likelihood. If the canvas needs a number, it comes over the wire from the fixture or, later, from stack 03a's world route. No backend files. No changes to `frontend/src/api/schema.ts` — that file belongs to stack 03a this cycle. No streaming (`spec/workbench/streaming-growth.md` is stack 04). No thesis card, no tail strip, no live prices.

**Rests on:** decision record 0007 (React Flow for the canvas, ELK for automatic layout, Motion for animation; own the look; no pop-ups), 0008 (the four testing layers). Read 0007's "Decision Outcome" — it is already a configuration list and this stack implements it.

**Read before writing a line of code:** `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §7 in full, all fourteen items UX-1 to UX-14. `spec/vocabulary.md`, especially the **Interface words** table — the six buttons and their badges are copied from it word for word and nowhere else. Then `docs/research/03-ui-ux-directions.md` §2, §3 and §5 for craft, with one correction: **that report recommends its "Instrument" direction, and Kent rejected the recommendation.** The look is the *Workbench* — decision D3 in `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §3: *the rigor of a visual-programming tool (boxes with typed sockets, wires that show the signal's shape) × cards rich with evidence you can pin and arrange like a mood board × a simulation game's sense of world state and time. Not minimalist; not a game.* The report's craft rules — typography, the two colour axes, the motion budget, the fourteen anti-patterns — all still apply.

**Runs in parallel with stack 03a (the engine).** Kent's decision D11.

---

## The four pull requests

Branch from `main`. Each pull request's base is the one above it.

| # | Branch → base | Contents |
|---|---------------|----------|
| 1 | `spec/03b-workbench` → `main` | **Docs only.** Six chapters: `spec/workbench/{tiles-ports-wires,layout-and-zoom,diff-view,inspector,color-motion-type,keyboard-and-access}.md`. Update the landing page's chapter table. **Amend `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` UX-6 and INV-12's row, and `spec/workbench/README.md`'s INV-12 row**, so provenance is carried by *a mark*, not *a stroke style* — see pull request 3. Three places, changed together. `streaming-growth.md` is stack 04 — do not write it |
| 2 | `feat/03b-canvas` → #1 | React Flow, the ELK worker, the custom tile, typed ports, the `WorldSource` seam, the launchpad. The Hormuz map draws |
| 3 | `feat/03b-wires` → #2 | Custom wires, the colour law and its tokens, the persistent Inspector, the path-product bar (INV-8) |
| 4 | `feat/03b-diff-and-keys` → #3 | Ghost overlay, delta rail, A ⇄ A′, the branch panel and UX-14, the keyboard map, reduced motion, the outline view, the end-to-end smoke test, the `e2e` job |

---

## Pull request 1 — the six chapters

Follow the chapter shape in `spec/README.md`: Purpose · Data model · Behaviour · INVARIANTS · ANTI-PATTERNS · Open questions. An interface chapter's "Data model" is the props a component takes and the tokens it reads; its "Behaviour" is worked examples on the Hormuz map. Every invariant names the test that checks it — a component test, or a line on the visual review checklist, which is itself a checkable thing.

The two invariants this part owns are **INV-8** (any displayed path shows the product of its link likelihoods beside the story) and **INV-12** (nothing is carried by hue alone: every direction has a glyph, every tail a texture, every provenance **a mark**). `keyboard-and-access.md` also owns the rendering rule that makes INV-7 visible: a chip never shows more than two significant figures and never omits its range.

`color-motion-type.md` carries **the colour law in one table**, and it is the chapter Kent will read first. Its organising rule is **one channel per meaning** — write that sentence into the chapter and into the writer's brief, because every failure in this area is two meanings fighting over one channel. The law: *likelihood rides brightness; direction of financial effect rides hue, blue up and amber down, always with a glyph and a sign; tail risk rides a hatch texture; **the kind of push rides the wire's stroke**; **provenance rides a mark at the wire's tail**; branch identity rides its own small palette and a name chip.*

**This refines two things already written, and pull request 1 must amend them rather than quietly diverge.** `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` UX-6 says "provenance → stroke style (`asserted` dashed)", its INV-12 row says "every provenance a stroke style", and `spec/workbench/README.md` repeats that wording. All three become **a mark**, because the stroke is now fully spent on the kind of push — a wire cannot be dot-dash for `impulse` and dashed for `argued` at the same time, and stack 02 already gave the stroke to the shape. The substance of UX-6 and INV-12 is unchanged: provenance is still visible on every wire, still without colour.

---

## Pull request 2 — canvas and tiles

**React Flow, and only its bare stylesheet.** `import "@xyflow/react/dist/base.css"` — never `style.css`, which carries the library's own look. A lint rule fails the `frontend` job if `style.css` appears anywhere (decision record 0007 promises this rule; write it).

**The tile.** A custom node type, **280 pixels wide**, height clamped, everything on the 8-pixel grid, hairline borders at 10% of the text colour, no shadows. It shows six things and no more:

1. The claim, wrapping to at most three lines then ellipsized — never truncated mid-word; the full text lives in the Inspector.
2. **Three belief chips** — model, user, market — as a three-up row. Each reads `.61 (.45–.75)`: two significant figures and the range, always. An empty `user` slot is a dash inviting a number. An empty `market` slot reads **no market** with its reason beside it, never a blank and never a placeholder number.

   **The range means one specific thing and the interface has to say which** (Kent, 2026-09-17, decision record 0014). It is *how sure we are of the number*, not *how much the world can move* — the second is already inside the likelihood. So the model chip's label is, word for word:

   > **model interval, uncalibrated** · how sure we are of `.35` — not how much the world can move

   and hovering it gives the sentence in full:

   > "Across 2 000 versions of this map — each one a set of numbers this model would have stood behind — the answer landed between .20 and .49 eight times in ten. Nobody has checked whether that 8-in-10 holds up; no claim on this map has resolved yet."

   Two things that sentence does on purpose: it says *eight times in ten* rather than naming a percentile, and it admits in its last clause that nothing is calibrated. Both are the product's honesty rule doing its job, and neither is optional.
3. Evidence clippings: at most two, each a letter monogram plus one line.
4. The resolve-by date.
5. A silhouette carrying `kind` — four of them, for `hypothesis`, `event`, `market`, `not_tradeable`. Shape carries the kind; hue never does.
6. Its badges, when it has any — see UX-14 in pull request 4.

**Typed ports.** One input group and one output group per tile, as React Flow handles. `trigger` and `sustain` wires attach to **distinct handle identifiers**, so what a wire means is visible at the socket before you follow it.

**ELK, off the main thread.** `elk.algorithm: layered`, `elk.direction: RIGHT`, `elk.layered.nodePlacement.strategy: NETWORK_SIMPLEX`, `elk.layered.crossingMinimization.semiInteractive: true`, `elk.layered.spacing.nodeNodeBetweenLayers: 120`, run in a Web Worker so layout never freezes the page. Already-placed tiles are pinned with `elk.position` so a later tile never reshuffles an earlier layer. `fitView` frames the map on first load only; after that `setCenter` follows the focused tile, because losing your place after a re-layout is anti-pattern 8 in the research. Cap seven tiles per layer and collapse the rest into a "+4 more" tile.

**Level of detail by zoom.** Below 0.6 zoom a tile becomes a summary — claim and belief chips only. Text never scales below 11 pixels; the tile changes representation instead of shrinking.

**Tiles do not drag.** Decision record 0007, and research anti-pattern 13: half-supported dragging looks broken. Pin, group and annotate arrive as explicit actions. Say so in the interface — a line in the keyboard sheet — rather than leaving a user to discover it by failing.

### The seam — `WorldSource`

Stack 03a is building the world route at the same time as this stack. The seam that keeps them apart:

```ts
export interface WorldSource {
  /** The base map and its branches, as the fixture route already serves them. */
  readBundle(id: string): Promise<FixtureBundle>;
  /** One world. Its numbers are OPTIONAL — see below. */
  readWorld(request: WorldRequest): Promise<WorldView>;
}
```

Two implementations. `FixtureWorldSource` reads `GET /api/fixtures/hormuz` and uses the fixture's stored `beliefs.model` for the base world — honest, because the fixture says in its own comments that those are illustrative. `ApiWorldSource` calls `POST /api/worlds` and `POST /api/worlds/diff`.

**And for the second world, before the engine exists, there is no second set of numbers at all** (Kent, 2026-09-17). No committed illustrative file, no hand-written likelihoods, no "illustrative numbers" chip. Numbers nobody computed are exactly the state a user cannot trace, and a plan that ships them for one stack ships them.

**What the diff view shows instead is structure, and structure is real.** It is computed from the branch — which this stack already has, because the fixture serves it — and it needs no arithmetic whatsoever:

| State | Computed from the branch by |
|---|---|
| `added` | The claim arrives in an `insert` |
| `killed` | The claim is the target of a `do(…, false)`, or the edits leave it with no path from the hypothesis |
| `downstream` | The claim is in the affected set of at least one edit — it is a claim your change can move |
| `untouched` | Everything else. Byte-identical, and the canvas can say so with confidence |

That is a genuinely useful view on its own: *"here is what your edit can reach, and here is what it provably cannot"* is the product's central correctness claim made visible, and it is the half of the diff that does not depend on the engine at all. Following arrows is **reachability, not arithmetic** — no strength is added, no likelihood is moved — so it does not break this stack's rule. When 03a lands, the server's `affected_set` is the authority and the browser's version becomes a hint that must agree with it; a component test pins the two against the Hormuz branch.

So every number slot in `WorldView` is optional, and an absent number **renders as an absence with a reason** — *"no engine yet"* in this stack, *"no market"* for an unpriced claim, a dash inviting your own number for an empty user slot. Never a blank, never a zero, never a placeholder. When 03a's route merges, switching to `ApiWorldSource` fills those slots and adds the fifth state, `shifted`; nothing is deleted, because nothing false was written.

`WorldView` is this stack's own view model in `frontend/src/world/types.ts`, written by hand — **not** generated from `schema.ts`, which belongs to stack 03a this cycle.

**The launchpad.** The empty state, and no illustration: the four example hypotheses from `ASSIGNMENT.md` as one-click cards, plus the Explore / Verify pair visible and explained in one line each. Only the Hormuz card opens a map in this stack; the other three say what they will do and are visibly not yet live — never silently inert.

---

## Pull request 3 — wires, the colour law, the Inspector

**Wires are custom edges**, drawn with `getSmoothStepPath` and a midpoint chip through `EdgeLabelRenderer`. **The stroke says one thing and one thing only: what kind of push this is** (Kent, 2026-09-17). Five encodings, each readable without colour:

| What | How |
|---|---|
| Signal shape | Stroke pattern: `impulse` dot-dash · `step` solid · `ramp` a gradient along the stroke |
| Strength | Stroke width, from `|strength|`, regardless of sign. Four steps, not a continuous ramp |
| `sustain` versus `trigger` | A `sustain` wire is double-stroked. A `trigger` wire is single |
| `reflexive` | The wire loops back on itself and carries a **lag chip** reading the delay in days |
| Provenance | **An origin mark at the wire's tail**, where the arrow leaves its cause — not the stroke. Three steps: **●●●** `documented`, `historical`, `market_implied` · **●●** `argued`, `user` · **●** `asserted`, `simulated`. The exact word is in the Inspector |

**Why provenance left the stroke.** One channel cannot carry two meanings. The stroke already says `impulse` or `step` or `ramp`, and stack 02 gave it that job; asking it to also say `argued` or `documented` means a dot-dash-and-dashed wire that says neither clearly. A three-step mark at the tail says the useful thing at a glance — *is there a document behind this, or is it the model talking* — and the seven-way distinction, which nobody reads off a picture anyway, lives in the Inspector where there is room for the word. Build it as one small component, `OriginMark`, used by the wire and by the Inspector so the two can never disagree. INV-12 still holds: provenance is visible on every wire and no hue is involved.

**The midpoint chip** shows the conditional likelihood in the arrow-and-bar idiom the forecasting site Metaculus uses: the target's likelihood **with this arrow's source supposed true**. That number is **not computed here** and it is **not on the world** — stack 03a computes it lazily, one arrow at a time, through `POST /api/worlds/conditional`, because computing all of them costs a whole extra propagation per arrow. So the canvas asks for it when a wire is hovered or selected and caches the answer. Until it has one — and always, in this stack, since the route does not exist yet — the chip shows the arrow's push read back in words, *"+1.6 · a strong push toward"*, which is data already on the link and needs no arithmetic. **Never a guessed number.**

**The colour law**, in one place, as CSS custom properties added to `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css` under a clearly marked new block. No existing token changes value.

| Axis | Channel | Tokens |
|---|---|---|
| Likelihood | Brightness — a five-step luminance ramp | `--p-0` … `--p-4`, each with its contrast ratio in a comment, as every existing token has |
| Direction of financial effect | Hue **plus a glyph plus a sign**, never hue alone | `--dir-up` (blue, ▲) and `--dir-down` (amber, ▼), both already in `tokens.css` |
| Tail risk | Texture | `--tail`, the hatch already in `tokens.css` |
| The kind of push | Stroke pattern, width and doubling | `impulse` dot-dash · `step` solid · `ramp` gradient; width from `|strength|`; `sustain` doubled |
| Provenance | **A mark, not a stroke** | The three-step origin mark at the wire's tail, above (Kent, 2026-09-17) |
| Branch identity | Its own small palette, on lanes and chips only — never on a tile's meaning | Violet, teal, rose, slate (*decided here*, accepted 2026-09-17). **Not amber**: amber already means "downward", and one hue cannot mean two things |

**The hover lens.** Hovering a tile dims everything not on its ancestor-or-descendant path to 15%. The research calls this the single highest-value interaction for legibility, and it is four lines of state.

**The Inspector is a persistent side panel and there are no pop-ups** (UX-10). It shows, for a claim: the full text, the resolution criteria and adjudicating source, the resolve-by date, the base rate with its reference class and its `k` of `n`, all three beliefs with owners, the evidence list, and — when the world carries one — the decomposition that makes the number explicable: *prior, then one line per incoming arrow with its push and its reason, then the result.* `spec/graph/belief.md` §B4 draws that block; copy its layout. **Reserve a slot directly under the range for "why is this band wide?"** — the answer is one sentence naming the claim whose own prior explains most of it (*"92% of this band is B's own starting number; pin that down and the band goes from 29 points to 8"*), it is computed from `World.range_shares`, and **it ships in stack 06, not here.** Leave the slot, leave a comment naming `range_shares`, render nothing. For an arrow: the rationale, the strength read back in words ("+1.6 — a strong push toward"), the mode in words, the lag, the shape, the sources with the day each was fetched, and the provenance in full — the word, with the same `OriginMark` the wire draws, so the mark and the word are one component and cannot drift apart.

**The path-product bar (INV-8).** Select a claim and a bar shows the multiplied-out likelihood of the path from the hypothesis to it, beside the story sentence. The product arrives on the world; this stack renders it. If it is absent, the bar says "no path shown" — it never multiplies anything itself.

---

## Pull request 4 — two worlds, the branch panel, the keyboard

**The ghost overlay.** Lay out the union of both worlds **once**, then draw the new world at full opacity and the old at 20% opacity, dashed, in the same coordinates. One layout, two paintings.

Each tile carries a diff state and that state drives its styling. In this stack there are four, all computed from the branch: `added` is solid with an accent ring; `killed` is ghosted, struck through, desaturated; **`downstream`** is drawn live — the claim your edit can reach, its number slot reading *"no engine yet"*; `untouched` is neutral, and it is the state the canvas can assert with confidence, because locality is a proven property and not a guess. The fifth state, `shifted` — `.61 → .18` with a directional chevron — arrives with the engine and needs no other change. **Never animate the diff as a crossfade** — `Space` toggles A ⇄ A′ as a hard switch, and the transition is scrubbable.

**The delta rail** sits beside the canvas. With the engine it is the terminal changes, ranked, one line each — *"the Polymarket Brent contract · .61 → .18 ▼ · largest on Oct 9"* — in the order the engine gave them, with **two columns that are never folded into the rank**: `range_width` (how unsure we are of the number) and **`agreement`** (the share of the 2 000 versions of the map that moved the same way — the vocabulary's reserved word for a number computed from how far independent runs differed, never self-reported). They answer different questions and a trader weighs them separately, which is why they are columns. Before the engine lands, **both columns render as an absence with its reason**, like every other number slot in this stack. **This stack does not rank and does not compute**: until the engine lands, the rail lists the terminals your edit can reach, in map order, each with an absence and a reason where the number will go. A rail that invented an ordering would be inventing the one thing the rail exists to tell you.

**UX-14, the overridden assertion.** A claim the user supposed true and that a later edit pushed back down never renders as plainly true. Its tile carries both states in order:

> **Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2 · by "a confirmed military strike on Iranian territory"**

**While a claim is supposed, its tile shows the word where a likelihood would go** — *Supposed · Oct 1*, not `1.0` and not `.98`. The engine treats a supposition as a hard fact in every draw (stack 03a, Kent's decision of 2026-09-17), so there is no number to show, and inventing one would answer a question the user did not ask.

Its series then carries three named states after that, and the tile and the time axis both read them: **supposed** → **withdrawn** (the supposition has been undermined and no opposing push has arrived yet — labelled *"withdrawn — no live push yet"*) → **pushed**. On the Hormuz branch that is Oct 1 supposed, Oct 2 to Oct 4 withdrawn at `.35`, Oct 5 onward pushed to about `.07`. The three-day gap between the badge's date and the day the number moves is the honest shape of the answer, and the interface must be able to say so rather than smoothing it away.

Every part of that line is data on the world, not inference: the assignment gives *Supposed* and its date; the retraction gives the date, the arrow and the claim to name; `states` gives the three-state series. The **branch panel** lists that branch's edits in the order they were made, each with the badge its operation earns, so the surprising rule reads as a sequence rather than as a number that moved on its own.

**The six buttons and badges, word for word from `spec/vocabulary.md`'s Interface words table** — copy them, do not paraphrase, and never show a code name:

| Button | Badge afterwards |
|---|---|
| **Suppose this is true** (and **Suppose this is false**) | **Supposed · date** |
| **This happened** | **Happened · date** |
| **Add a claim** (hinted "…but this also happens") | **Added** |
| **Change this push** | **Retuned** |
| **Split this claim** | **Split** |
| **My own number** | none — the three-up belief chip is the badge |

and the derived one no button produces: **Retracted · date · by "…"**.

In this stack the buttons **build a branch and show it**; they do not move a number, because moving numbers is the engine's job. **My own number** and **Change this push** append an edit to the branch and the branch panel shows it immediately. **Split this claim** is visibly not yet live and says so (stack 06).

**The keyboard map (UX-9).** `⌘K` command palette · `j`/`k` between siblings · `h`/`l` along wires between layers — arrow movement follows the *wires*, not screen space · `E` intervene · `B` branch · `Space` A ⇄ A′ · `?` the shortcuts sheet. Focus is always visible, using `--focus`. Everything reachable by keyboard alone, end to end.

**Reduced motion (UX-7).** The motion budget is three animations and no more: the propagation wave (wires draw in causal order, about 200 milliseconds, staggered 60 milliseconds down the map), branch creation, and the belief number-roll. Everything else is at most 120 milliseconds of opacity. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` the **ordering survives and the tweening goes** — per-layer instant reveals, a number swap instead of a roll, a hard cut instead of a ghost transition. Never remove the ordering: the ordering is the causality.

**The outline view (UX-12).** The map also exists as a nested list with `role="tree"`, each item read as a sentence — *"Brent crude settles below $68 for five sessions, 61 per cent likely, caused by the war-risk premium falling"*. A re-propagation announces itself through `aria-live="polite"`: *"Branch created. Six claims changed, one retracted."*

**Tests** (decision record 0008, layer 4):

- `frontend/src/graph/__tests__/layout.test.ts` — pinned tiles keep their positions across an incremental layout; the union layout used for a diff is stable.
- `frontend/src/graph/__tests__/diffState.test.ts` — the reducer maps a base map plus a branch to the four structural states, and the claim the strike branch provably cannot reach comes out `untouched`.
- `frontend/src/world/__tests__/branchReducer.test.ts` — the intervention panel appends edits in order and never edits one in place.
- `frontend/src/components/__tests__/beliefChip.test.tsx` — **`test_chip_never_shows_more_than_two_significant_figures`**, that the range is never omitted, that an absent number renders its reason, and that a supposed claim renders the word rather than a likelihood. This is decision record 0005's promised frontend rendering test; it is the one test that holds NFR-1 up.
- One end-to-end browser test with Playwright: open the Hormuz map, the tiles draw, open the strike branch, downstream tiles change and the fully separated claim does not, and H's tile reads *Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2 · by "…"*.
- A fifth continuous-integration job, `e2e`, running that one test. **No API key in it** (INV-13).

---

## Pre-decisions — settle nothing twice

Pasted in full into every brief on this stack. **Kent, 2026-09-17** marks an answer Kent gave after an independent review of this plan; *decided here* marks a small choice this plan took and Kent accepted in the same review. Nothing on this page is still open.

| Topic | Decision |

| Provenance | **Kent, 2026-09-17: a mark, not a stroke.** A three-step origin mark at the wire's tail — ●●● `documented`/`historical`/`market_implied` · ●● `argued`/`user` · ● `asserted`/`simulated` — with the exact word in the Inspector. One component, `OriginMark`, used by both. Pull request 1 amends UX-6 and INV-12 to say "a mark" |

| The second world, before the engine | **Kent, 2026-09-17: structure only.** `added` · `killed` · `downstream` · `untouched`, computed from the branch. **No committed illustrative world and no chip.** Every number slot in `WorldView` is optional and an absent number renders as an absence with a reason. `shifted` arrives with the engine |
| The midpoint chip | **Kent, 2026-09-17.** The conditional is the *supposed* number, computed lazily by the engine one arrow at a time. Until it is fetched, the chip reads the push in words ("+1.6 · a strong push toward"). Never a guess |

---

## Sub-agents and waves

Seven Opus sub-agents. Each in its own git worktree under `../katalyst-wt/<branch>/`, committing on its branch, and **never pushing, never opening a pull request, never touching `main`**. The coordinator reviews by running the commands and *looking at the screen* itself.

### The waves

| Wave | Agent | Branch → base | Owns, and only these | Parallel with |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | *coordinator* | `spec/03b-workbench` → `main` | Creates the branch with six chapter stubs (headings only) committed, so the code worktree can branch off immediately | — |
| 0 | **W1** | shared worktree `spec-03b` | `spec/workbench/tiles-ports-wires.md`, `spec/workbench/color-motion-type.md` | W2, W3, C |
| 0 | **W2** | shared worktree `spec-03b` | `spec/workbench/layout-and-zoom.md`, `spec/workbench/keyboard-and-access.md` | W1, W3, C |
| 0 | **W3** | shared worktree `spec-03b` | `spec/workbench/diff-view.md`, `spec/workbench/inspector.md` | W1, W2, C |
| 0 | **C** | `feat/03b-canvas` → the stub commit | `frontend/src/graph/**`, `frontend/src/world/**`, `frontend/src/components/Tile*`, `frontend/src/components/Launchpad*`, `frontend/src/App.tsx`, `package.json` | W1–W3 |
| 1 | **R** | read-only over `spec-03b` | The six chapters against each other, `vocabulary.md`, `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §7, decision record 0007. Reports inconsistencies; the coordinator fixes | V |
| 1 | **V** | `feat/03b-wires` → `feat/03b-canvas` | `frontend/src/graph/wires/**`, `frontend/src/components/OriginMark*`, `frontend/src/components/Inspector*`, `frontend/src/components/PathBar*`, `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css` (the new block only) | R |
| 2 | **K** | `feat/03b-diff-and-keys` → `feat/03b-wires` | `frontend/src/graph/diff/**`, `frontend/src/components/DeltaRail*`, `frontend/src/components/BranchPanel*`, `frontend/src/keyboard/**`, `frontend/src/a11y/**`, `frontend/e2e/**`, `frontend/playwright.config.ts`, `package.json` and `package-lock.json` (the one Playwright dependency), `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `ARCHITECTURE.md` §1 and §7 | — |

**Two lines that must reach their writers' briefs.** W1 (`color-motion-type.md`): *one channel per meaning* is the chapter's organising rule, and provenance is a mark rather than a stroke. W3 (`inspector.md`): the panel reserves a slot for **"why is this band wide?"**, whose one-sentence answer comes from `World.range_shares` and **ships in stack 06** — the chapter describes the slot and says plainly that it is empty in this stack.

**W1–W3 share one worktree, have disjoint files, and run no git commands** — the coordinator commits for them, exactly as the chapter writers worked in stack 02. The chapter stubs go in first so agent C can branch and start while Kent still has reading to do.

**Three code agents, not one.** Unlike the engine, the canvas splits cleanly: tiles and layout, then wires and the colour law, then two worlds and the keyboard. Each layer is visible on screen before the next starts, which is what lets Kent's eye be the test — and his eye is the only test for this stack that matters.

### The two shared files

Identical to the rule in `stack-03a-engine.md`, and in every brief on both stacks:

1. **`frontend/src/api/schema.ts` belongs to 03a.** No agent here runs `make types`. A `schema.ts` diff on a 03b branch is a mistake to be reverted. This stack does not need the world types: it types its own view models behind `WorldSource`.
2. **`ARCHITECTURE.md` is split by section.** 03a writes §3, §5, §10; 03b writes §1 and §7, in pull request 4 only. Whichever stack merges second re-applies its own sections after `git merge origin/main`.

Everything else is disjoint: 03b is `frontend/**` plus `spec/workbench/**` plus `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; 03a is `backend/**` plus `spec/multiverse/**`.

### The brief every agent gets

Same nine parts as the engine stack, with four differences:

1. **The two vetoes are the point of this stack**, not a footnote. Paste them and paste D3's sentence about what the Workbench is.
2. **Read first:** `AGENTS.md`; this plan's section for your pull request; decision record 0007; `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §7 in full; `spec/vocabulary.md` including the Interface words table; `spec/workbench/README.md`; `docs/research/03-ui-ux-directions.md` §2, §3, §5 — **with the correction that the report's "Instrument" recommendation was rejected.**
3. **Verify before reporting:** `npm run check`, then use the `run` skill to launch the app and **capture screenshots of every state you built** — empty, loaded, hovered, selected, diffed, keyboard-focused, reduced-motion, light theme. Attach the file paths to your report. An agent that reports "it looks good" without pictures has not finished.
4. **The pre-decisions table above, pasted in full.**

### The coordinator's review, after every agent

- [ ] `git diff --stat` against the owned-files list; **no `schema.ts` diff, no `backend/` diff**
- [ ] `npm run check` run by me in the worktree
- [ ] `package.json` diff read: no dependency beyond the four named above
- [ ] Launch the app myself and walk every state — do not review from the agent's screenshots alone
- [ ] Run the veto checks below
- [ ] Read every string on screen against `spec/vocabulary.md`; no code name, no internal number, no jargon
- [ ] Commit messages: type, scope, co-author line
- [ ] Write the pull request body (*What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*); open with `gh pr create --base <parent>`
- [ ] Append `STATUS.md`

### The veto checks — run these on every screenshot

Kent vetoes a template-looking interface on sight, so the coordinator looks for the template first.

1. Does anything look like a component library's defaults — a rounded blue button, a drop shadow, a system font stack, a default focus ring?
2. Is there a spinner anywhere? A pop-up? A dialog you have to dismiss? Any of the three is a veto.
3. **Convert the screenshot to greyscale.** Does every arrow still say what kind it is and where it came from, every direction still read up or down, every tail still show as texture? If not, INV-12 is broken.
4. Is any number on screen showing more than two significant figures, or missing its range?
5. Is there a number whose origin cannot be named in one click? Is there a number nobody computed — an empty slot filled in rather than left as an absence with a reason?
6. Is the map layered left to right, or is it a hairball with crossings?
7. Is any text below 11 pixels? Is any text under 4.5 to 1 contrast, in either theme?
8. Is the tile 280 pixels wide and on the 8-pixel grid? Measure it, do not eyeball it.
9. Tab through the whole screen with the keyboard only: is focus always visible, and does arrow movement follow the wires?
10. Turn on reduced motion: is the ordering still there and the tweening gone?
11. Are the six buttons and badges word for word the Interface words table?
12. Does a claim that was supposed and then overridden say so on its tile?

### The gate

**M3b** — stack 03b complete: four pull requests open and green; the Hormuz map draws, wires carry their five encodings, the Inspector answers "why", two worlds lay over each other, UX-14 renders, the keyboard works end to end, the `e2e` job is green. Kent has looked at it and nothing triggered a veto.

**M3** is both gates: the engine computes it and the canvas shows it. Stack 04 joins them by switching `WorldSource` to `ApiWorldSource`, which fills the empty number slots and adds the fifth diff state. Nothing is deleted at that point, because nothing false was written.

content.text: Now the engine chapters. Reading `propagation.md` and `diff.md` in full.

content.content:
1	# Propagation — how a change travels
2	
3	## Purpose
4	
5	A branch is a list of edits; a world is what those edits do to the numbers. This chapter is the arithmetic in between. After it, the user can suppose the strait opens, insert a strike the next day, and watch one claim after another move on the days they actually move — and click any number to see the prior it started from and the pushes that were added to it. It settles four things the rest of the product has been deferring: **when** each claim's clock starts, **how** a likelihood is computed on a given day, **how a supposition ends** when a later edit undermines it, and **what the range under a computed number means**. The last one is the reason the range stopped being decoration: it says *how sure we are of the number*, not how much the world can move, and it no longer shrinks when the machine is given more computer time.
6	
7	Everything here rests on decision record **0014** (accepted 2026-09-17) — *a supposition ends when something pushes back; a range says how sure we are of the number, not how the dice fall* — and on record 0005 (log-odds pushes, trigger and sustain, seeded simulation), which 0014 amends in three places without superseding.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Data model
12	
13	Written by pull requests 2 and 3 of this stack, in `backend/src/katalyst/domain/patch.py` and `backend/src/katalyst/domain/propagation.py`. Frozen, like everything else in `domain/`: no clock, no network, no global state.
14	
15	### What `apply` hands to `propagate`
16	
17	`apply` folds a branch's edits onto a base map, in order, and returns **the map it leaves behind together with every value an edit fixed**:
18	
19	```python
20	def apply(
21	    graph: Graph,
22	    branch: Branch,
23	    assignments: tuple[Assignment, ...] = (),
24	) -> tuple[Graph, tuple[Assignment, ...]] | list[Violation]
25	```
26	
27	```python
28	class Assignment(BaseModel):          # frozen, like everything in domain/
29	    target: PropositionId             # the claim an edit fixed
30	    value: bool                       # what it was fixed to
31	    at: date | None                   # the day it holds from; None means day zero
32	    by: int                           # which edit did it: its position in the branch, counting from 0
33	    kind: Literal["do", "observe"]    # which of the two verbs the user chose
34	```
35	
36	**`Proposition` grows no "fixed value" field, and never will.** A fixed value is a fact about a *world*, not about a claim. Written onto the claim, the same claim would mean different things in different branches and the base map would stop being the one thing every branch agrees on ([`branches-and-worlds.md`](branches-and-worlds.md), open question 1, decided 2026-09-17). The pair — map and assignments — is also what a further `apply` takes, which is what keeps the concatenation law type-checking (INV-5: applying two branches in a row equals applying the two joined).
37	
38	The list stays **ordered** so a later assignment reads as overriding an earlier one rather than silently replacing it. That ordering is what the tile's *Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2* line is drawn from (UX-14 in `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §7).
39	
40	### What a claim's day looks like
41	
42	```python
43	SeriesState = Literal["sampled", "supposed", "withdrawn", "pushed"]
44	# sampled   — the ordinary case: no supposition has ever touched this claim
45	# supposed  — a `do` is holding; the claim is true in every draw and the tile shows a word
46	# withdrawn — the supposition has been undermined and no opposing push has arrived yet
47	# pushed    — an opposing push is live
48	```
49	
50	```python
51	class Retraction(BaseModel):
52	    target: PropositionId    # the claim whose supposition ended
53	    at: date                 # the day it ended — the day the opposing arrow's SOURCE became true
54	    by_link: LinkId          # the arrow that undermined it
55	    by_claim: PropositionId  # that arrow's source — the claim the tile names in its badge
56	    by: int                  # the edit that introduced the arrow, by position in the branch
57	```
58	
59	### What a world is
60	
61	```python
62	class World(BaseModel):                                   # frozen
63	    base_id: str
64	    branch_id: BranchId | None
65	    seed: int
66	    versions: int                                         # the outer loop — how sure we are of the inputs
67	    worlds: int                                           # the inner loop — how the dice fall
68	    day_zero: date
69	    days: int                                             # the window's length in whole days, not the number of series points
70	    graph: Graph                                          # the map apply left behind
71	    assignments: tuple[Assignment, ...]
72	    retractions: tuple[Retraction, ...]
73	    beliefs: Mapping[PropositionId, Belief]               # owner "model", read on each claim's resolve-by day
74	    series: Mapping[PropositionId, tuple[float, ...]]     # one likelihood per day, for the time axis
75	    states: Mapping[PropositionId, tuple[SeriesState, ...]]  # one named state per day, same length as the series
76	    conditionals: Mapping[LinkId, Belief]                 # empty by default — see below
77	    range_shares: Mapping[PropositionId, Mapping[PropositionId, float]]
78	                                                          # whose prior explains whose band; no route reads it until stack 06
79	    warnings: tuple[str, ...]                             # plain sentences; the low-survival warning lives here
80	```
81	
82	`series` is what makes the scrubbable time axis possible (UX-3), and `states` is what lets the canvas say *Supposed* where a number would mislead and *withdrawn — no live push yet* where a number would confuse. Every entry in `beliefs` is owned by `model` and is read on that claim's own resolve-by day — INV-1 guarantees every claim has one, so there is always such a day, and it is the day the claim is judged. Which day a *change list* row is read on is a different question and belongs to [`diff.md`](diff.md).
83	
84	**`conditionals` means *supposed*, not *observed*, and it is empty on a freshly built world.** The number on a wire's midpoint chip is the target's likelihood **with that arrow's source supposed true** — a `do`, the interventional number. It is never "how often do these two show up together", which is the correlational quantity [`../graph/link.md`](../graph/link.md)'s anti-pattern 3 refuses; putting that on a wire claiming a mechanism would be the worst kind of quiet lie. Computing it costs a whole extra propagation per arrow — eight on the Hormuz map, about eighty on a sixty-claim one — for a number most users never open, so it is fetched **lazily**, one arrow at a time, through `POST /api/worlds/conditional`. Laziness costs nothing in honesty: the number is a pure function of the same three inputs plus the arrow, so a lazily fetched number is byte-identical to an eagerly computed one.
85	
86	### The one entry point
87	
88	```python
89	def propagate(
90	    graph: Graph,
91	    assignments: tuple[Assignment, ...],
92	    *,
93	    as_of: date,
94	    seed: int,
95	    versions: int = 2_000,   # the outer loop: versions of the map (how sure we are of the inputs)
96	    worlds: int = 8,         # the inner loop: worlds per version (how the dice fall)
97	) -> World
98	```
99	
100	Sixteen thousand worlds in total, about **ten milliseconds at sixty claims**. The two numbers are not interchangeable; they measure two different kinds of not-knowing, and B5 below says which is which.
101	
102	**Three things that are deliberately absent.** There is no `strength_lo` and no `strength_hi`, now or ever: link strengths are **fixed numbers in stack 03a** and only priors vary between versions. Widening an arrow is derived from its `provenance` — "how well-backed" becomes "how wide" — and that ships in stack 04, where arrows finally differ from one another; every arrow in today's fixture is hand-written `argued` or `asserted`, so doing it now would widen everything by the same amount and teach nobody anything. There is no `scipy`: the Latin hypercube — a way of spreading draws evenly instead of letting them clump — is three lines of `numpy`, and the percentiles are one. And there is no module-level random generator — see B7.
103	
104	---
105	
106	## Behaviour
107	
108	Worked on the Strait of Hormuz map. Its claims, quoted from the fixture word for word:
109	
110	| | The claim | `prior` |
111	|---|---|---|
112	| **H** | *The Strait of Hormuz reopens to unrestricted commercial transit.* — the hypothesis | `.35 (.22–.50)` |
113	| **C** | *Lloyd's war-risk insurance premium for Gulf transits falls below 0.4%.* | `.30 (.18–.45)` |
114	| **B** | *Brent crude settles below $68 for five sessions.* | `.28 (.15–.42)` |
115	| **R** | *OPEC+ announces output restraint.* — the tail | `.18 (.08–.32)` |
116	| **M1** | *A Polymarket contract "Brent below $70 on 2026-10-31" resolves YES.* — tradeable | `.40 (.28–.55)` |
117	| **M2** | *The energy fund XLE underperforms the S&P 500 fund SPY by more than 3% over 20 trading days.* — tradeable | `.35 (.22–.50)` |
118	| **N1** | *Omani-mediated United States-Iran talks resume publicly.* — real, and no venue prices it | `.22 (.12–.36)` |
119	| **S** | *A confirmed military strike on Iranian territory.* — on the branch only | `.06 (.02–.14)` |
120	
121	Day zero is 2026-10-01.
122	
123	Every number below is **illustrative**, exactly as the fixture's are, and pull request 3 may tune the fixture's inputs to make the example richer (each tuned value carrying a comment saying what it was, what it is and why). The golden test therefore asserts **directions and orderings**, never these values.
124	
125	### B1 — The time axis: day zero, the window, and the day a claim is settled
126	
127	**Day zero is `as_of`**, passed in by `engine/worlds.py` from the stored example's `fixture_date`. `Graph` grows no date field. The window runs from day zero to the latest `resolution.by` date on the map, in whole days. Every date becomes an integer day index at the edge of `propagate` and stays an integer inside it.
128	
129	**Every claim gets a day on which it is *settled*** — the day its clock starts, so that any arrow leaving it measures elapsed days from there. Three rules, in order:
130	
131	1. If an assignment fixes it, that day is the assignment's `at` (day zero when `at` is `None`).
132	2. Otherwise it is the earliest day any live incoming arrow reaches it: the day that arrow's source was settled, plus the arrow's `lag`.
133	3. A claim with neither an assignment nor a live incoming arrow is settled on **day zero** — the map carries no timing information about it, so its clock starts at the beginning of the window.
134	
135	**Being settled is not being true.** A claim with no assignment is sampled from its own `prior`, every draw, exactly as always; nothing is ever forced true because its clock started. The two ideas are separate and conflating them is the mistake this paragraph exists to prevent. It follows that the settled day — call it `t_source` — is **one schedule, computed once from the shape of the map**, the same in every draw, while **truth is per draw**: an arrow's term is non-zero only in those draws where its source came out true. One schedule, sixteen thousand different worlds running along it.
136	
137	**The window is capped at 180 points.** If the window is longer than 180 days the series is sampled down to 180 evenly spaced points and a sentence in `warnings` says so. `states` is always the same length as `series`.
138	
139	> **On the Hormuz map.** The longest resolve-by date is R's and N1's, sixty days out, so the window is sixty days and the cap never bites. On the strike branch, H is settled on day 0 by `Do(target="H", at=2026-10-01)` and S on day 1 by `Do(target="S", at=2026-10-02)`. C is settled on day 0, because `H → C` carries `lag=0.0`. B is settled on **day 1**: `S → B` carries `lag=0.0` and S was settled on day 1, so that arrow reaches B the same day — earlier than `H → B`'s two-day lag (day 2), `R → B`'s five (day 5) or `C → B`'s seven (day 7). In the base world, where there is no S, B is settled on day 2 via `H → B`. B's own clock is what the arrows *leaving* B measure from, so on the branch M1 is settled on day 2 (`B → M1`, one-day lag) and M2 on day 4 (`B → M2`, three-day lag), each a day earlier than in the base world. R is settled on **day zero**: its only incoming arrow is `B → R`, the feedback arrow, and this stack sets reflexive arrows aside rather than unrolling them (stack 06 does that), so R has no live incoming arrow and rule 3 applies.

141	### B2 — One claim's log-odds on one day
142	
143	At day *t*, for each claim, in an order that always puts causes before effects — a topological order, with reflexive arrows set aside exactly as `validate` already sets them aside for its loop check (INV-6: a map has no loops once feedback arrows are removed):
144	
145	```
146	log-odds(claim, t) = baseline(claim) + Σ over live incoming arrows: strength × shape(t − t_source)
147	```
148	
149	`baseline(claim)` is the log-odds of the claim's own `prior` — its likelihood before anything causes it. *Log-odds* is the natural logarithm of the chance a claim is true divided by the chance it is false; it is the scale on which independent pushes **add** instead of multiplying, which is why a claim with three parents gets three numbers added together rather than a table of eight combinations. Where a formula below needs it by name, the log-odds of a likelihood `x` is written `logit x`, and the way back — log-odds to a likelihood between 0 and 1 — is written `sigmoid`.
150	
151	`shape` is a plain function of **elapsed days**, and it is zero before the cause is settled. Writing `u` for `t − t_source` and `L` for the arrow's `lag`:
152	
153	```
154	impulse(u) = 0                          for u < L        zero through the lag, then a spike
155	             2 ** (−(u − L) / half_life)    for u ≥ L    that halves every half_life days
156	
157	step(u)    = 0                          for u < L        zero through the lag, then
158	             1                          for u ≥ L        full size, held
159	
160	ramp(u)    = u / L                      for 0 ≤ u < L    climbing from 0 to 1 across the lag,
161	             1                          for u ≥ L        then full size, held
162	```
163	
164	**`lag` is the ramp's rise time**, and there is no `rise_time` field in version 1. That settles [`../graph/link.md`](../graph/link.md)'s open question 5. A `half_life` on a `step` or a `ramp` is a **violation**, not an ignored field — the thirteenth code, `half_life_without_impulse`, already on `main`; this stack cites it and does not add it again. Reject, never repair.
165	
166	**A warning above ±5.** `validate` is untouched and puts no ceiling on `strength`; an unbounded number is the honest type. But ±5 is roughly 1% to 99% on a coin flip, so `propagate` adds a plain sentence to `warnings` naming any arrow beyond it. A warning, not a rejection: the map is still legal, and the user should be told.
167	
168	> **On the Hormuz map.** B's prior is `.28`, whose log-odds is `−0.94`. On the strike branch, day 1: `S → B` is an impulse with `lag=0.0`, so it is already at full size — `−2.4`. `H → B` has not arrived (two-day lag); `C → B` has not arrived (seven-day lag); `R → B` has not arrived (five days from R's day zero). Total `−0.94 − 2.4 = −3.34`, about **`.03`**. Day 2: `H → B` arrives at full size, `+1.6`, and `S → B` has faded by one day of its ten-day half-life to `−2.24`. Total `−1.58`, about **`.17`**. B *rises* between day 1 and day 2, and that rise is golden assertion 4.

170	### B3 — Trigger and sustain, as arithmetic
171	
172	Both kinds of arrow use the same formula. They differ in one clause, and it is the whole domino-and-apple distinction:
173	
174	* A **sustain** arrow's term is **zero on any day its source is not true**. The desk is gone; the apple falls.
175	* A **trigger** arrow's term **keeps running on its own schedule once fired**, whatever the source does afterwards. The domino stays fallen.
176	
177	Nothing else differs. The two behave identically for as long as the cause holds, and part company the day it stops. [`../graph/link.md`](../graph/link.md) draws it:
178	
179	```
180	                   t0                      t1
181	                   │                       │
182	trigger (domino)   ▼                       ▼
183	push on effect ────█████▇▇▆▆▅▅▄▄▃▃▂▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁
184	                   └ fires once, then fades on its own;
185	                     t1 changes nothing — the domino stays fallen.
186	
187	sustain (apple on desk)
188	push on effect ────████████████████████████▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁
189	                   └ holds while the cause holds …
190	                                           └ … and is gone at t1.
191	
192	t0 = the cause becomes true.    t1 = the cause stops being true.
193	The cause is the link's `source`; the effect is its `target`. Elsewhere
194	these two are also called the parent and the child.
195	```
196	
197	And the three shapes, so the two pictures can be read together:
198	
199	```
200	                   cause true             lag ends
201	                   │                      │
202	impulse  push  ────┴──────────────────────█▇▆▅▄▃▂▁▁▁▁▁   spike, then halves every half_life
203	step     push  ────┴──────────────────────██████████████   switches on and holds
204	ramp     push  ────┴▁▁▁▂▂▂▃▃▃▄▄▄▅▅▅▆▆▆▇▇▇▇██████████████   climbs across the lag, then holds
205	```
206	
207	> **On the Hormuz map.** `H → B` is a trigger that fired on day 0, so on day 2 it delivers `+1.6` to B even though H's supposition was withdrawn on day 1 — that domino is down. `H → C` is a sustain, so from day 1 its `+1.1` is present only in the draws where H still came out true, which after day 4 is about seven in a hundred. Same cause, two honest behaviours, one branch.

209	### B4 — How a supposition ends
210	
211	**A supposition is a hard fact until something undermines it.** While a `do` holds, the claim is simply **true in every draw** — not a large log-odds baseline that arrows can argue with. There is no ±4.0, no `.98`, no number at all: the tile shows the word *Supposed* and its date where a likelihood would go. That is what "suppose this is true" means in English, and a tool that answered "suppose this is true" with `.98` would be lying about what the user asked for.
212	
213	**It stops holding on the day the *cause* of the first live opposing arrow becomes true.** Not the day that arrow's push reaches full size — the day the world changed. An arrow into the target is *opposing* when its push runs against the value that was supposed: negative strength against a claim supposed true, positive against one supposed false. In code: `Retraction.at = t_source` of that arrow's source, and the arrow's own `lag` then does its ordinary work afterwards. From that day the claim is computed like any other claim: its own prior, plus every live arrow, each arriving on its own schedule.
214	
215	Tying the end of a supposition to the *arrival* instead would tie "do I still take your word for this" to a delay parameter — change a lag from three days to thirty and the supposition silently outlives the news.
216	
217	> **On the Hormuz strike branch, with day zero at 2026-10-01:**
218	>
219	> | Days | What `H` reads | Why |
220	> |---|---|---|
221	> | Oct 1 | **Supposed · Oct 1** — a word, not a number | The `do` holds; `H` is true in every draw |
222	> | Oct 2 – Oct 4 | **`.35`**, the series marked *withdrawn — no live push yet* | `S` became true on Oct 2, so the supposition is withdrawn that day. `S → H` carries `lag=3`, so nothing is pushing yet and `H` falls back to its own prior |
223	> | Oct 5 onward | **about `.07`**, the series marked *pushed* | `S → H`'s step reaches full size — `−1.9` on a log-odds baseline of `−0.62` — and pushes `H` down |
224	>
225	> The tile reads *Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2 · by "a confirmed military strike on Iranian territory"* — UX-14's badge, with the claim named in the fixture's own words — and the world carries one `Retraction` with `at=2026-10-02`, `by_link="S->H"`, `by_claim="S"`. The three-day gap between the date on the badge and the day the number moves is **not a bug to hide**. It is the honest shape of the answer, and the series has to be able to say so — which is exactly why every day carries a named state.
226	>
227	> One hair's-breadth detail, so nobody reads it as a bug: on the withdrawn days H reads its prior of `.35`, and the reported number comes out `.36`. B5 says why.
228	
229	**The rejected alternatives**, one line each, kept for the record. *A permanent seal* — the user's first edit would silently veto their third; [`interventions.md`](interventions.md) rejected it on 2026-09-17, and it deletes the showcase. *A large finite baseline the arrows argue with* — at ±4.0 an arrow of `−1.9` moves the claim from `.98` to `.89`, which is not a retraction, and it makes "suppose" mean "assume ninety-eight per cent", which is not what the button says. *Hold until the push lands* — that is the delay-parameter trap above, and it is a cliff with no state in between.

231	### B5 — The two kinds of not-knowing, and where the range comes from
232	
233	Read this before any formula, because it is the idea the whole design rests on.
234	
235	* **How the dice fall.** The strait either opens or it does not. That is already inside `p`: `p` is the share of worlds in which the claim came out true.
236	* **How sure we are of the numbers we put in.** Every prior on the map was elicited, and a different but equally defensible set of priors would give a different `p`. **That** is the range.
237	
238	So a wide band means *"we are not sure what number to give you; more homework would move it"* — never *"the event is more volatile"*. That is the one sentence a trader has to be able to repeat, and the chip says it: **model interval, uncalibrated · how sure we are of `.35` — not how much the world can move.** The formal name for two loops of this shape — one for how sure we are of the inputs, one for how the dice fall — is a second-order, or two-dimensional, Monte Carlo.
239	
240	**What a stated `{p, lo, hi}` means: a split logit-normal** — a bell curve on the log-odds scale with its two halves fitted separately: middle `p`, 10th percentile `lo`, 90th percentile `hi`. "Eight times in ten" is the phrase. The halves are fitted **on the log-odds scale**, the scale the pushes add on:
241	
242	```
243	s_lo = (logit(p) − logit(lo)) / 1.2816        # 1.2816 is the 90th percentile of a standard normal
244	s_hi = (logit(hi) − logit(p)) / 1.2816
245	```
246	
247	`logit x` is the log-odds of `x`, defined in B2; `sigmoid` is the way back — it turns log-odds into a likelihood between 0 and 1.
248	
249	Version *k* draws one standard-normal number `z` per stated range and reads the prior back as `sigmoid(logit(p) + z × s_lo)` when `z` is negative and `sigmoid(logit(p) + z × s_hi)` when it is positive. Separately, because real elicited ranges are lopsided: over the seven base-map claims the fixture's own ranges are near-symmetric on log-odds (mean gap ratio 0.94) and clearly skewed on probability (1.24). This honours all three stated numbers exactly, stays inside 0 and 1 with no clamping, and needs no new field on `Belief`.
250	
251	**One consequence, written here rather than left for a reader to trip over.** The mean of a split logit-normal sits slightly above its median when `p < .5`. So a claim's `prior.p` and its computed `beliefs.model.p` differ by a hair *even for the hypothesis, which has no causes*: H is `.35` as a prior and `.36` as a computed belief. Both are right. [`../graph/belief.md`](../graph/belief.md)'s `prior` versus `beliefs.model` table says so too.
252	
253	**The loop.**
254	
255	1. Draw **2 000 versions** of the map with a Latin hypercube over every prior's fitted shape. `numpy` only, three lines. A version is **one coherent set of numbers this model would have stood behind**, never "every low end at once".
256	2. Inside each version, run **8 worlds**.
257	3. **Keep the likelihood, not the coin flip**: for each claim keep the likelihood it came out true in that world. Free variance reduction — the number is already computed. (The textbook name for this is Rao-Blackwellisation.)
258	4. **Correct for inner noise** with the law of total variance (the rule that a total spread is the spread of the averages plus the average of the spreads — so subtract the second), so that what is left is the spread across versions and not the spread across eight coin flips. Writing `q` for the 2 000 version-level answers and `inner_var` for the spread of the eight likelihoods inside a version:
259	
260	```
261	f = sqrt(max(0, 1 − mean(inner_var / worlds) / var(q)))
262	q_corrected = mean(q) + (q − mean(q)) · f
263	```
264	
265	5. `p` is the mean over both loops. With no `observe` on the branch that is the same number as `mean(q)`, because every version runs the same number of worlds; with an `observe` it is the survival-weighted mean of B6, and the recentring above uses that same weighted mean. `lo` and `hi` are the 10th and 90th percentiles of the corrected version-level values. `f` is clamped at 0, so a claim whose apparent spread was all noise reports a zero-width band rather than an imaginary number.
266	
267	**Measured, on Hormuz claim B at day 45, against the exact answer by enumeration — `.35 (.20–.49)`:**
268	
269	| Design | Reports | Wobble of the band edges across seeds |
270	|---|---|---|
271	| Three runs: all lows, then all highs | `.19–.50`, and it is not a bound — `R → B` is negative, so the true corner is `.158–.567` | none |
272	| 20 batches of 500 | `.25–.46` — a quarter of that width is coin-flip noise, and the band is 28% too narrow | ±.021 |
273	| The analytic delta method — calculus instead of sampling: work out how much each stated range moves the answer, and add those up | `.22–.52`, accurate to .004, but fifty times slower and first-order only | none |
274	| **2 000 × 8, likelihoods kept, noise-corrected** | **`.20–.50`** | **±.002 to ±.003**, about 10 ms at 60 claims |
275	
276	The delta method is kept — not as the engine, but as a **cross-check in a test**.
277	
278	**Where the width comes from, free.** From the same outer sample, sorting the versions into bins by the value each prior drew, and comparing the bins' averages, gives each claim's **share of another claim's band** — how much of the width comes from not being sure of *this* claim. Six lines of `numpy`, nothing run twice. It is carried as `range_shares[target][source]` — the share of `target`'s band explained by `source`'s prior — and **no route reads it until stack 06**, where it becomes FR-21's "where to spend modeling budget" ranking. It is computed and carried now because the sample it comes from is thrown away otherwise. On the fixture, **92% of B's band is B's own prior**; pin that down and the band goes from 29 points to 8, while everything else contributes less than half a point. (FR-21 and record 0014 say "its own base rate"; the thing that varies between versions is the claim's `prior`, which is the word used here.)
279	
280	**Two counter-intuitive warnings, both measured.**
281	
282	* **A `do` does not reliably narrow what is downstream.** It collapses the target's own band, but B's width went *up* under `do(H)` — `.292` to `.323` — because the logistic curve is steeper near `.45`. The honest thing to show is the **share**, not the width: H's contribution to B's band went from 2.6% to 0%.
283	* **A terminal's band is dominated by its own prior.** An upstream range reaches it multiplied by `p(1−p)`, which is at most a quarter. Do not build the demo around "widen H and watch B widen"; it moves about 4%.
284	
285	### B6 — `observe`: keep only the consistent draws
286	
287	`observe` records that a claim actually came true or false. Unlike `do` it cuts nothing, and it is handled in the **inner** loop: inside each version, keep only the worlds in which the claim came out as observed, then **weight that version by its survival share** when the two loops are pooled. Five lines of importance weighting — a version under which the observation was likely counts for more than one under which it was a fluke.
288	
289	**This is why observing reaches upstream and supposing does not.** Throwing worlds away changes what the survivors say about the claim's *causes* just as much as what it *causes* — which is exactly why `observe`'s affected set under INV-4 (locality: an edit changes only what is still connected to its subject in the map the edit leaves behind) includes its ancestors and their descendants, while `do`'s does not. INV-3 (assert is not observe) is the product-level statement of the same thing, and the two operations are never merged into one "set this value" control.
290	
291	**Below about two per cent survival the world carries a loud warning, and the warning says the *range* is unreliable, not merely the point.** A version that survived twice out of eight is contributing a very noisy number to the band, and the noise correction can only subtract what it can measure.
292	
293	> **On the Hormuz map.** `Observe(target="C", value=True)` — the premium printed below 0.4% this morning — keeps only the worlds in which C came out true. C's own cause is H, and the surviving worlds are the ones where H more often came out true, so H rises: cheap insurance is evidence the lane really is open. `Do(target="C", value=True)` on the same claim leaves H exactly where it was. That difference is the product.
294	
295	### B7 — Two seed streams, and replay
296	
297	Everything comes from the one `seed` argument, through `numpy.random.Generator` objects built from it and nothing else. **No module-level generator, no clock, no global state, ever.** The same `(map, branch, seed)` gives byte-identical worlds on any machine — NFR-2, the determinism requirement — which is what makes a three-day-old screenshot reproducible from three values.
298	
299	There are **two streams**, and keeping them apart is load-bearing:
300	
301	| Stream | Drives | Rule |
302	|---|---|---|
303	| `params` | The outer loop — which 2 000 versions of the map we try | **Must not depend on the branch.** A base world and a branch world built from the same seed use the *same* 2 000 versions |
304	| `worlds` | The inner loop — how the dice fall inside one version | Ordinary; may depend on anything |
305	
306	The `params` rule is what makes a difference between two worlds readable. Compare a base world and a branch world version by version and the only thing that changed is the edit — the numbers underneath were held fixed. That is *common random numbers*, and without it every comparison is the user's change plus a wash of sampling noise, which is exactly the failure [`branches-and-worlds.md`](branches-and-worlds.md)'s anti-pattern 4 describes. [`diff.md`](diff.md) spends the whole of it: a change is read off the paired difference, never off whether two bands overlap.
307	
308	> **On the Hormuz map.** Supposing the strait opens, B's two bands **overlap by a third** — and yet **100% of versions move the same way**, `+.10`, with a 10-to-90 band of `+.07` to `+.13`. Band overlap would report "no change" about the single clearest change on the map.
309	
310	### B8 — What the user ends up looking at
311	
312	One `propagate` call fills every field of `World`. On the Hormuz strike branch, with the fixture's seed `20261001`:
313	
314	| What the interface reads | Where it comes from |
315	|---|---|
316	| The number on a tile | `beliefs[claim]`, read on that claim's own resolve-by day, rendered at two significant figures with its range (NFR-1) |
317	| The sparkline and the scrubber | `series[claim]`, one point per day, so the spike and the fade are visible rather than hidden (UX-3) |
318	| *Supposed* / *withdrawn — no live push yet* / *pushed* | `states[claim]`, the same length as the series |
319	| The **Retracted · date · by "…"** badge | `retractions`, which names the day, the arrow and the claim (UX-14) |
320	| The number on a wire's midpoint chip | `conditionals[link]`, fetched one arrow at a time, and always the *supposed* number |
321	| Sentences under the map | `warnings` — low survival, a sampled-down series, a strength beyond ±5 |
322	
323	Four of those are what the golden test checks, and each is a sentence a person can read back: the strike lowers B; the strike makes **C less likely** (`C` is the claim *"Lloyd's war-risk insurance premium for Gulf transits falls below 0.4%"* and `S → C` is `−2.0`, so the shorthand "the premium stays high" means C goes **down** — getting this backwards silently inverts the test); H is *supposed*, then *withdrawn*, then *pushed*; and B **rises** between day 1 and day 2, because what already fell stays fallen.

343	**INV-multiverse.9 — the versions do not depend on the branch.** For all maps `g` from `graphs()`, all branches `b` from `branches(g)` and all seeds `s` from `seeds()`: the 2 000 versions drawn for a base world and for a branch world from one seed are element-for-element identical. Without this, every comparison is the user's edit plus a wash of sampling noise. Test: `test_versions_do_not_depend_on_the_branch`. Replay across both streams is `test_same_seed_same_world`, above, which compares two runs of the *same* inputs and so cannot see this. Checked from the other side in `backend/tests/unit/domain/test_diff.py` by `test_shifted_needs_agreement` ([`diff.md`](diff.md) owns that statement). *Catches:* deciding that something moved by comparing two bands — a pair of worlds whose bands overlap heavily but which move the same way in every version must come out `shifted`, not `unchanged`.
344	
345	**INV-multiverse.10 — a supposition is true in every world until it is undermined.** For all maps `g` from `graphs()` and all `Do` edits from `interventions(g)` against which no live opposing arrow exists: the target comes out true in **every** one of the 16 000 worlds, and its state on every day is `supposed`. Not `.98`, not `.999`. Test: `test_supposition_is_true_in_every_world_until_undermined`. *Catches:* an implementation that models a supposition as a large finite baseline.
346	
347	**INV-multiverse.11 — a retraction dates from the cause, not from the push.** For all maps `g` from `graphs()` and all branches from `branches(g)` that undermine a supposition: each `Retraction.at` equals the day the opposing arrow's **source** was settled, and never that day plus the arrow's `lag`. Test: `test_retraction_dates_from_the_cause_not_the_push`. *Catches:* tying "do I still take your word for this" to a delay parameter.
348	
349	**INV-multiverse.12 — the band is not sampling noise.** For all maps `g` from `graphs()` rewritten so that every prior is a point — `lo = p = hi` — and all seeds `s`: every computed band comes out **essentially zero width**, within tolerance. Test: `test_band_is_not_sampling_noise`. *Catches:* reporting coin-flip spread as uncertainty, which is the single most likely way to get this chapter wrong.
350	
351	**INV-multiverse.13 — the band agrees with an independent method.** Not a generated statement: it is pinned to the shipped Hormuz fixture at the fixed seed. The sampled band agrees with the analytic first-order (delta-method) band to two significant figures. Two independent methods, one answer; it is what keeps the delta method useful after it was rejected as the engine. Test: `test_range_matches_analytic_first_order_on_fixture`. *Catches:* a band that is the right shape and the wrong size.
352	
353	**INV-multiverse.14 — the domino stays fallen and the apple falls.** For all maps `g` from `graphs()` containing a `trigger` arrow whose source is later reset: the target's series after the reset is byte-identical to the series in which the source was never reset. For all maps containing a `sustain` arrow: on every day its source is not true, its term is exactly zero. Tests: `test_trigger_persists_after_parent_reset`, `test_sustain_retracts_when_parent_removed`.
354	
355	**INV-multiverse.15 — propagation is idempotent and order-independent.** For all maps `g` from `graphs()`, all assignment lists and all seeds `s`: propagating a second time over the same inputs gives a byte-identical world; and shuffling the ties in the causes-before-effects ordering — the claims no arrow orders relative to one another — gives a byte-identical world. Tests: `test_propagation_idempotent`, `test_propagation_order_independent`.
356	
357	**INV-multiverse.16 — a starved observation warns, and says the range is unreliable.** For all maps `g` from `graphs()` and all `Observe` edits from `interventions(g)` under which fewer than two per cent of worlds survive: the world carries a warning whose sentence says the **range** is unreliable, not merely the point. Test: `test_observe_warns_below_two_percent_survival`.
358	
359	**INV-multiverse.17 — the Hormuz map reads the way the story reads.** Not a generated statement: it is pinned to the shipped fixture at the fixed seed `20261001`, four assertions, each one a sentence a person can check. Test: `test_hormuz_strike_branch_reads_the_way_the_story_reads`, in `backend/tests/unit/fixtures/test_hormuz_golden.py`.
360	
361	| # | Assertion |
362	|---|---|
363	| 1 | **The strike lowers Brent-below-$68.** `B`'s likelihood on its resolve-by day is lower in the strike branch than in the base world |
364	| 2 | **The strike keeps the war-risk premium up.** `C` is the claim *"Lloyd's war-risk insurance premium for Gulf transits falls below 0.4%"* and `S → C` is `−2.0`, so the strike makes `C` **less** likely. The roadmap's shorthand "raises the premium claim" means the premium stays high, which is `C` going **down**. Read the wording before writing the assertion |
365	| 3 | **The strait's standing is withdrawn, and the push lands three days later.** `H`'s state is `supposed` on day 0, `withdrawn` on days 1 to 3 with a series reading about `.35`, and `pushed` from day 4 with a series below `.10`. The world carries one `Retraction` for `H` with `at` = 2026-10-02, `by_link` = `S->H`, `by_claim` = `S` |
366	| 4 | **What already fell stays fallen.** `B`'s series **rises** between day 1 and day 2 — the strike has already hit it, and then `H → B`'s trigger arrives on its two-day lag and pushes back the other way. A world in which `B` only ever falls has lost the domino |
367	
368	Directions and orderings, never values: research report 02 §3 reports `P(M1)` going from about `.61` to about `.18` and `P(M2)` from about `.54` to about `.09`, and the fixture's own numbers differ. The same report writes `H → B` as `−1.6` because it was thinking about the oil *price*; the fixture writes `+1.6` because `B` is the *claim* "Brent settles below $68", and the sign is on the claim. The fixture is right.
369	
370	---
371	
372	## ANTI-PATTERNS
373	
374	**1. Do not report the spread of the coin flips as the band.** *Because* it measures the machine rather than the map: run more worlds and the "uncertainty" shrinks, which means a number that moves when you buy computer time is being passed off as a statement about the world. **Do** run two loops, subtract the inner noise with the law of total variance, and take the percentiles across versions — and keep `test_band_is_not_sampling_noise`, which freezes every prior at a point and demands a zero-width band.
375	
376	**2. Do not let the `params` stream see the branch.** *Because* the base world and the branch world then run on different underlying numbers, and every comparison becomes the user's edit plus a wash of elicitation noise, with no way to separate them. **Do** derive `params` from the seed alone, so version *k* of both worlds was built from the same numbers and the difference is the edit.
377	
378	**3. Do not model a supposition as a big finite baseline.** *Because* ±4.0 is an arbitrary constant with no source; it contradicts the user in about two per cent of worlds; an opposing arrow of `−1.9` moves the claim from `.98` to `.89`, which is not a retraction; and it makes "suppose this is true" mean "assume ninety-eight per cent", which is not what the button says. **Do** make the claim true in every draw while the supposition holds, show a word where a number would go, and end it on the day the opposing cause becomes true.
379	
380	**4. Do not fit `{p, lo, hi}` on the probability scale.** *Because* elicited ranges are lopsided there — over the seven base-map claims the fixture's are skewed 1.24 on probability and near-symmetric 0.94 on log-odds — so a symmetric fit has to clamp at 0 and 1 and silently stops honouring the three numbers the model actually stated. **Do** fit the two halves separately on the log-odds scale, which honours all three exactly and can never leave 0–1.
381	
382	**5. Do not decide that something moved by comparing two bands.** *Because* the bands answer a different question. Under `do(H)` on the fixture, B's two bands overlap by a third while 100% of versions move the same way — band overlap would report "no change" about the clearest change on the map. **Do** subtract version by version and read the paired difference; [`diff.md`](diff.md) states the rule and `test_shifted_needs_agreement` pins it.
383	
384	**6. Do not reach for a module-level random generator, a global seed, or the clock.** *Because* a world would then depend on how many other worlds had been computed before it, which quietly destroys replay (NFR-2: the same map, branch and seed give byte-identical worlds) and with it every reproducible screenshot. **Do** pass the seed as an argument, build every `numpy.random.Generator` from it, and let `test_world_replays_from_base_branch_seed` fail loudly if anyone slips.
385	
386	**7. Do not type a computed number by hand.** *Because* a hand-written `beliefs.model` cannot say why it is what it is, which is the traceability veto exactly. **Do** set the fixture's `beliefs.model` equal to its `prior` — the truthful statement "nothing has been computed yet" — and serve the engine's world beside the map. Every number in a demo comes from the engine or from a recording of the engine.
387	
388	**8. Do not put "how often these two show up together" on a wire.** *Because* that is a correlation, and a wire claims a mechanism; the two disagree whenever a third thing caused both, and the reader has no way to tell. **Do** compute `conditionals` with the arrow's source **supposed** true — a `do` — exactly as [`../graph/link.md`](../graph/link.md)'s anti-pattern 3 requires.
389	
390	**9. Do not add `strength_lo` and `strength_hi` to make arrows uncertain.** *Because* every arrow in today's fixture is hand-written `argued` or `asserted`, so spreading them now would widen everything by the same amount and teach nobody anything — and a second elicited pair per arrow is exactly the budget record 0005 refused. **Do** keep strengths fixed in 03a and derive the spread from `provenance` in stack 04, where "how well-backed" becomes "how wide" at no extra elicitation cost.
391	
392	---
393	
394	## Open questions
395	
396	Raised 2026-09-17. Each needs Kent.
397	
398	1. **An `impulse` that names no `half_life`.** [`../graph/link.md`](../graph/link.md)'s open question 4 settled one direction — a half-life on a `step` or a `ramp` is a violation — and left this one open: an `impulse` with `half_life=None` is legal today, and the shape above has no decay to evaluate. Three candidates, none picked here: read it as no decay at all (which makes the arrow a `step` and quietly ignores the author's choice of shape), take a default from somewhere, or make it a fourteenth violation code. It does not bite in stack 03a because every `impulse` in the fixture names a half-life — `B → M1` carries a comment saying it was added for exactly this reason — but `propagate` has to do *something* the first time a generated map omits one.
399	
400	2. **Which arrow the badge names when two undermine a supposition on the same day.** The rule is "the first live opposing arrow", and the fixture has exactly one. If two opposing arrows' sources are settled on the same day, `Retraction.by_link` needs a stated tie-break — the larger push, the earlier edit, or the smaller identifier — or the badge is not deterministic, which would break replay.
401	
402	3. **A `ramp` with `lag = 0.0`.** The shape divides by the lag, so a zero-lag ramp has no rise time. Reading it as "full size on the same day" makes it a `step`, which is probably right and is certainly better than a division by zero — but it means two shapes describe one behaviour, and nothing today says so out loud.
403	
404	4. **A second `do` on a claim whose supposition has already been withdrawn.** Assignments are ordered and a later one overrides an earlier one, so the user can re-suppose a retracted claim. Does the second supposition hold from its own date until undermined again — giving a series that reads *supposed · withdrawn · pushed · supposed* — and does the world then carry two retractions for one claim? The shapes allow it; nothing has decided what it means.
405
